PENDING-1776-01:
April 19, 1775… midnight alarm.
No cap. Farmers woke up kings.
Liberty or death. God first, then the clip.
Let’s ride.
Midnight hoofbeats thunder, Revere cuttin’ through the dark,
Lanterns in the steeple—two if by sea, we spark.
Plows left in the furrow, wives clutchin’ babies tight,
These ain’t soldiers, just men who knew wrong from right.
Concord powder stash, British boots comin’ for the steel,
Seventy Minutemen step to the green, hearts of chilled steel.
Parker stands tall, voice steady through the fear:
“Don’t fire first, boys—but if they want it, make it clear.”
Redcoats in formation, bayonets catch the dawn,
Farmers in homespun, muskets older than their sons.
First shot cracks the silence—nobody knows who lit the fuse,
But that spark lit a fire no empire could ever use.
Embattled farmers! Standin’ on God’s sovereign ground,
Liberty above all but the throne where the King is crowned.
Blood on the North Bridge, smoke in the April breeze,
We fired the shot heard round the world—now the tyrants on their knees!
No king, no crown, no chain gon’ break these hands,
We die for the free, leave the farm for the free man’s stand.
Sovereignty eternal, etched in every grave we fill—
God, then liberty, or we die where we build!
Lexington Green turned red, brothers droppin’ in the dew,
Eight good men gone before the sun even knew.
But we fell back swingin’, regrouped at the rude bridge arch,
Barrett, Buttrick, Davis—Acton boys lead the charge.
Smoke from the town, they thought we burnin’ our own,
Four hundred farmers marched like the devil’s own storm.
British volley hit first—then we answered with hell,
Isaac Davis dropped, but his men still gave ’em the swell.
Redcoats break and run, militia harrowin’ the road,
Every rock, every tree, every farm boy unload.
Wives watch from windows, tears mixin’ with pride,
Knowin’ if they don’t come home, at least their sons ain’t gonna hide.
Picture the sacrifice—last kiss at the door at 2 a.m.,
Man whispers to his daughter, “Daddy fightin’ for your amen.”
Fields he tilled for years now soaked in patriot red,
Mothers bury husbands while the church bells still bled.
They wasn’t seekin’ glory, wasn’t chasin’ no throne,
Just ordinary men who refused to bow to the unknown.
No more stamps, no more tea, no more chains on the free,
God gave us these rights—kings don’t get to decree.
From the bridge to Bunker Hill, from the blood to the pen,
They planted the seed of a nation that’ll never bend again.
Every scar on that road, every unmarked grave in the grass,
Screams: sovereignty first—after God, we never ask.
We the embattled. We the unheard. We the spark.
Farmers turned gangsters when the empire went too dark.
No retreat, no surrender, no compromise on the soul—
Liberty in our veins, sovereignty carved in stone.
Above all but the Father who breathed life in our chest,
We stood on that green so the future could rest.
Embattled farmers! Echo through the centuries loud,
Liberty sovereign—God’s gift, never bowed!
Shot heard round the world still ringin’ in the air,
Every free breath we take? They paid for it there.
Rest in power, you legends in homespun and grit—
We ride for the same flag. We never gon’ quit.
April 19… forever.
Embattled farmers.
Gangsters for God and the free.
The end of kings. The birth of we.
PENDING-1776-02:
The Tree of Liberty stands sentinel in time's deep soil,
An ancient elm once rooted near Boston's crowded way,
Where in sixteen forty-six its seed took hold,
And by seventeen sixty-five became the people's stage.
Beneath its boughs the Sons of Liberty gathered first,
Hanging effigies of tyrants in the August heat,
Stamp Act's shadow cast, yet resistance nursed—
A living arbor where free voices dared to meet.
No idle emblem, this: the tree bore copper plate,
Inscribed with liberty's defiant claim,
While British axes later felled its state
In seventeen seventy-five, to feed their flame.
Yet metaphor endures beyond the severed trunk—
Jefferson, from Paris in seventeen eighty-seven's fall,
Wrote to Smith of Shays' uprising, blunt:
The tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time
With the blood of patriots and tyrants. It is its natural manure.
Not lightly spoken, this agrarian truth—
Liberty as organism, requiring sacrifice to thrive,
Not perpetual bloom without cost or ruth,
But cyclical renewal where the vigilant strive.
Roots draw deep from revolution's fertile ground,
From Concord's shot that echoed round the world,
From Yorktown's siege where freedom's sound
Rang out in cannon's roar, banners unfurled.
Branches reach through centuries, scarred yet unbowed—
Through fratricide and global fire we stand,
Each drop of blood, each vow avowed,
Sustains the canopy across the land.
Roots draw from revolution's fertile ground,
From Concord's shot heard round the world,
From Yorktown's siege where freedom's sound
Echoed in cannon's roar, banners unfurled.
Branches reach through centuries, scarred yet unbowed:
Through Civil War's fratricide, where brothers bled to mend,
Through world conflagrations, where the proud
Stood against total darkness, refusing to bend.
In quieter vigils too—the ballot cast in shadow,
The courtroom plea for rights long denied,
The solitary stand when crowds grow shallow—
Each drop sustains the canopy worldwide.
We tend it now not with romantic fire,
But measured reverence for its fragile height:
Prune the overgrowth of complacency's mire,
Water with vigilance through the longest night.
For every generation inherits the charge—
To guard against the slow rot of power unchecked,
To nourish what was planted at such large
Cost, lest the tree wither, hollow, wrecked.
O tree of liberty, ancient and profound,
Your leaves whisper of endurance, not of ease;
In your shade we find both shelter and ground
For the fierce, quiet labor that keeps us free.
May we honor the manure of history's price,
Patriots' resolve and tyrants' fall,
And with steady hands, in sober sacrifice,
Refresh you still—lest freedom lose us all.
Refresh you still… lest freedom lose us all.
PENDING-1776-03:
Boston Harbor lay frozen under Parliament’s cruel decree,
Port Act slammed the gates shut—starvation on every quay.
Tea Party lit the spark, but the Crown answered with chains,
Five Intolerable Acts forged in London’s darkest flames.
Charter ripped to ribbons, elected men cast aside,
Town meetings gagged and broken, governors crowned with royal pride.
Judges shipped across the sea where justice wore a British face,
Quartered redcoats in our homes—tyranny in our own space.
Samuel Adams thundered through the streets of midnight fire,
Sons of Liberty rose like ghosts, fueled by righteous ire.
Joseph Warren penned the Resolves—“No obedience is due!”
One voice became a thousand, and the flame burned straight and true.
Paul Revere rode the darkness, warnings cutting through the night,
Minutemen grabbed their muskets, ready for the fight.
They boycotted, they united, they refused the tyrant’s hand—
From Boston’s broken harbor, defiance swept the land.
This is the Intolerable Flame—burning hotter than their lies!
We will not bow, we will not break, though the redcoats blacken the skies!
One small stand in the dirt became the roar that shook the throne,
Blood of patriots watering the tree that freedom calls her own.
No king, no act, no iron boot can chain what God made free—
We are the sons of seventy-four—untamed, wild, and free!
Philadelphia called the Congress—thirteen colonies stood as one,
Suffolk Resolves echoed loud: “These acts shall be undone!”
They pledged their lives, their fortunes, their sacred honor on the line,
Boycotts bit the British purse while the spirit rose like wine.
From the ashes of oppression came the powder-keg of might,
The shot heard round the world was born in that defiant night.
Today the Acts wear different names—ports of livelihood slammed shut,
Cities punished for their voice, rights stripped without rebut.
Officials shielded from the law, troops of power in our streets,
Foreign mandates in our homes where the Constitution bleeds.
But the flame still burns the same—history screams the warning clear:
When tyrants push too far, the people rise without fear!
This is the Intolerable Flame—roaring louder than before!
We will not bow, we will not break—liberty forevermore!
From Boston’s ghosts to your front door, the call rings loud and true:
Stand like the patriots of ’74—me and you!
One life, one stand, one raging heart can turn the darkest tide,
Water the tree with righteous blood—let freedom never die!
No chains can hold what God set free—rise up and claim your name…
The Intolerable Flame still burns—the Revolution lives again!
Hear the hammer of the blacksmith… hear the hoofbeats in the night…
The flame is in your blood tonight…
Rise.
